title: Bad Boys II
full_review:
Original bad boys Martin Lawrence and Will Smith reunite eight years after their first buddy-cop movie in the mindlessly violent action flick "Bad Boys II" (Columbia).
The protracted sequel, brought to the screen by producer Jerry Bruckheimer and director Michael Bay, visually assaults the audience with its senseless, slow-motion gunplay and explosions. With careening shots and whiplash cuts, Bay throws out one action sequence after another until they are a blur on screen. The film stretches on and on as the body count rises and the strained plot resembles a patchwork of incoherent scenes stapled together. And painted in broad strokes, the underdeveloped villains are silly caricatures.

Smith and Lawrence once again play Miami narcotics cops Mike and Marcus, this time after a Cuban drug lord (Jordi Molla with a perpetual three-day beard) smuggling millions of dollars worth of ecstasy pills into the United States. Gabrielle Union joins the duo as Marcus' sister, an undercover DEA agent going after the same target.

Missing is a zippy rapport that could have made Smith and Lawrence's comic scenes zing instead of fizzle. The sequel feels tired, and after so many long car chases and shootouts, so does the audience. The swaggering cops emerge from crushed cars and fiery explosions with nary a scratch, making the gruesome violence seem like just a game.

Loud, long and leaden, "Bad Boys II" may work at the box office, but let's hope most audiences will have had enough with the equally mind-numbing first one.

Because of relentless stylized graphic violence, a sexual encounter and some sexual innuendo, drug content and constant rough language with some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
